To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-1-infected individuals produce antibodies that bind to CD 43, a differentiation antigen on thymic T cells, but not on circulating T cells.
HIV-1-infected individuals produce autoantibodies against the differentiation antigen, CD43 (sialoglycoprotein), on thymic T lymphocytes.
HIV infection is associated with the production in the host of autoantibody specific for CD43.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of autoantigens that are recognized by autoantibodies in the sera of individuals infected with HIV-1.
the development of a new class of HIV-1 diagnostic tests that can identify the HIV-1 infected individual at the earliest possible time.
the study of the mechanisms of HIV-1 infection, with a particular emphasis on the role of autoantibody responses in HIV-1 disease progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV-1 infection is specifically and uniquely associated with the production and secretion of autoantibody that can recognize and bind to native T lymphocyte surface differentiation antigen.
HIV-1 infection is specifically linked to the development of a new class of autoantibody that binds to a T cell surface antigen that is not normally recognized by the immune system.
HIV infection leads to the production of auto- antibodies which recognize CD43, a molecule which plays an important role in the differentiation and activation of T cells.
